rows: P01 & \textbf{Baseline cooperation propensity}. Typical contribution level before accounting for responses to other participants' later behavior. & \citet{Ledyard1995}; \citet{Fischbacher2001} \\

P02 & \textbf{Costly contribution orientation}. Willingness to sacrifice own immediate material payoff through contribution when contribution is privately costly. This is a behavioral tradeoff, not a claim that altruism, efficiency, warm glow, or conformity is the cause. & \citet{Ledyard1995}; \citet{Fischbacher2001}; \citet{Andreoni1990}; \citet{CharnessRabin2002} \\

P03 & \textbf{Opportunistic withholding}. Withholding contribution while benefiting from substantial peer contribution, including late or situational exploitation. & \citet{Ledyard1995}; \citet{Fischbacher2001}; \citet{Andreoni1988} \\

P04 & \textbf{Peer-responsive cooperation}. Degree to which contribution changes in the same direction as observed peer cooperation or explicit cooperative coordination. & \citet{Fischbacher2001}; \citet{KeserVanWinden2000} \\
P05 & \textbf{Threshold cooperation}. Sharply changing contribution levels when peer cooperation crosses a salient level. & \citet{Fischbacher2001} \\
P06 & \textbf{Contribution volatility}. Within-game variability in contribution after accounting for clear peer-contingent responses. & \citet{Ledyard1995}; \citet{Chaudhuri2011} \\
P07 & \textbf{Directional learning trend}. Gradual directional change in contribution as rounds and experience accumulate. & \citet{Andreoni1988}; \citet{Chaudhuri2011} \\

P08 & \textbf{Withdrawal after adverse peer behavior}. Reduction in subsequent contribution after peer free riding, conflict, or another clearly adverse social event. & \citet{Fischbacher2001}; \citet{KeserVanWinden2000}; \citet{FalkEtAl2018} \\
P09 & \textbf{Recovery after peer improvement}. Restoration of contribution after peers resume cooperation or repair a negative interaction. & \citet{KeserVanWinden2000}; \citet{FalkEtAl2018} \\
P10 & \textbf{Endgame contribution change}. Direction of contribution change near the known or reasonably anticipated end of the game. & \citet{Andreoni1988}; \citet{Chaudhuri2011} \\
P11 & \textbf{Initial cooperative optimism}. Initial willingness to contribute before observing how much other participants contribute. & \citet{Fischbacher2001}; \citet{FalkEtAl2018} \\

P12 & \textbf{Exploitation sensitivity}. Behavioral sensitivity to being disadvantaged by low-contributing or higher-earning peers. & \citet{FehrSchmidt1999}; \citet{BoltonOckenfels2000}; \citet{CharnessRabin2002} \\
P13 & \textbf{Rule comprehension}. Accuracy and consistency in applying game and payoff rules. & \citet{HouserKurzban2002} \\
P14 & \textbf{Forward planning}. Evidence that current actions anticipate later rounds, future reactions, or consequences of the game rules. & \citet{Andreoni1988}; \citet{Chaudhuri2011} \\
P15 & \textbf{Punishment propensity}. Frequency and intensity of punishment when it is available. & \citet{FehrGachter2000} \\

P16 & \textbf{Low-contributor punishment selectivity}. Degree to which punishment is concentrated on lower contributors rather than applied indiscriminately. & \citet{FehrGachter2000}; \citet{HerrmannEtAl2008} \\
P17 & \textbf{Punishment direction}. Whether punishment is directed toward higher or lower contributors. & \citet{FehrGachter2000}; \citet{HerrmannEtAl2008} \\
P18 & \textbf{Cooperation response after received punishment}. Direction of the next contribution response after the player is punished. & \citet{FehrGachter2000}; \citet{Nikiforakis2008} \\
P19 & \textbf{Reward propensity}. Frequency and intensity of costly reward when it is available. & \citet{AndreoniHarbaughVesterlund2003}; \citet{SeftonEtAl2007} \\
P20 & \textbf{High-contributor reward selectivity}. Degree to which reward is concentrated on higher contributors. & \citet{AndreoniHarbaughVesterlund2003}; \citet{SeftonEtAl2007} \\

P21 & \textbf{Relationship-contingent reward}. Use of reward conditional on a specific partner's prior favorable treatment or reciprocal interaction. & \citet{AndreoniHarbaughVesterlund2003}; \citet{CharnessRabin2002} \\

P22 & \textbf{Cooperation response after received reward}. Direction of the next contribution response after the player receives reward. & \citet{AndreoniHarbaughVesterlund2003}; \citet{SeftonEtAl2007} \\
P23 & \textbf{Chat engagement}. Frequency of participation when a communication channel is available. & \citet{Sally1995}; \citet{Balliet2010}; \citet{BochetEtAl2006} \\
P24 & \textbf{Coordination leadership}. Attempts to initiate, organize, or stabilize a group contribution plan. & \citet{KoukoumelisEtAl2012}; \citet{BochetEtAl2006} \\
P25 & \textbf{Commitment making}. Making or eliciting explicit nonbinding promises about future contribution. & \citet{KerrKaufmanGilliland1994}; \citet{KoesslerEtAl2021} \\
P26 & \textbf{Cooperation-norm appeals}. Invoking fairness, duty, reciprocity, or a cooperation norm to influence the group. & \citet{HaruvyEtAl2017}; \citet{BochetEtAl2006} \\

P27 & \textbf{Responsive and affiliative communication}. Directly responding to others while maintaining a supportive, appreciative, or rapport-building tone. & \citet{HaruvyEtAl2017}; \citet{Balliet2010} \\
P28 & \textbf{Blame and conflict escalation}. Use of accusation, shaming, hostility, or escalating interpersonal conflict. & \citet{HaruvyEtAl2017}; \citet{BochetEtAl2006} \\
P29 & \textbf{Repair communication}. Apologizing, acknowledging error, conceding, or attempting to restore cooperation after a rupture. & \citet{BottomEtAl2002} \\

P30 & \textbf{Message-action inconsistency}. Degree to which claims, promises, or strategic messages conflict with later observable action. & \citet{KerrKaufmanGilliland1994}; \citet{KoesslerEtAl2021}; \citet{BottomEtAl2002} \\

rows: C01 & \textbf{Own-surplus protection}. Consistency with which choices protect or increase the participant's payoff, calculated using their assigned private chip values. & \citet{Nash1950}; \citet{MurphyEtAl2011} \\

C02 & \textbf{Integrative trade search}. Tendency to construct or support packages that plausibly create gains for both sides using participant-visible evidence. & \citet{Nash1950}; \citet{CharnessRabin2002}; \citet{ChakrabortyHarbaugh2003} \\

C03 & \textbf{Preference for equal exchange quantities}. Preference for equal or nearly equal quantities of chips on both sides of an exchange, regardless of private chip values. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{KagelEtAl1996}; \citet{FehrSchmidt1999} \\

C04 & \textbf{Relative-outcome concern}. Concern with avoiding disadvantage or seeking an advantage relative to others, beyond absolute own surplus. & \citet{FehrSchmidt1999}; \citet{BoltonOckenfels2000}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995} \\
C05 & \textbf{Proposal claim level}. How much the participant seeks to gain from proposed trades, given the available chips. & \citet{Nash1950}; \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{RothEtAl1991} \\

C06 & \textbf{Acceptance-calibrated offer adaptation}. Degree to which proposals become more likely to be accepted after observed responder feedback. & \citet{Rubinstein1982}; \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995} \\
C07 & \textbf{Package breadth}. Preference for exchanging larger multi-chip packages rather than small packages, given the available chips. & \citet{ChakrabortyHarbaugh2003} \\
C08 & \textbf{Exchange-ratio simplicity}. Preference for simple equal-count or low-complexity exchange ratios. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{ChakrabortyHarbaugh2003} \\

C09 & \textbf{Inventory and option-value planning}. Use of current holdings in ways that preserve or create later bargaining opportunities. & \citet{Rubinstein1982}; \citet{ChakrabortyHarbaugh2003} \\
C10 & \textbf{Own-surplus acceptance threshold}. Minimum gain the participant requires to accept an offer. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995}; \citet{RothEtAl1991} \\
C11 & \textbf{Profitable-offer uptake}. Reliability of accepting offers that clearly increase the participant's payoff under their private chip values. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{KagelEtAl1996} \\

C12 & \textbf{Fairness-motivated rejection}. Rejection attributable to visible unfairness or exploitation even when the participant would gain. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995}; \citet{KagelEtAl1996}; \citet{FehrSchmidt1999} \\

C13 & \textbf{Strategic rejection and delay}. Rejecting currently acceptable terms to seek better later terms, conceal information, or discipline proposers. & \citet{Rubinstein1982}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995} \\

C14 & \textbf{Counterpart-value belief updating}. Revising offers or responses as observed proposals, acceptances, rejections, and changes in chip holdings reveal information about other participants' private chip values. & \citet{KagelEtAl1996}; \citet{ChakrabortyHarbaugh2003} \\

C15 & \textbf{Counterparty-contingent adaptation}. Adjusting later behavior according to which bargaining partner previously accepted, rejected, proposed favorable terms, or held relevant chips. & \citet{RothEtAl1991}; \citet{KagelEtAl1996} \\

C16 & \textbf{Relationship conditioning strength}. Strength of later favorable or unfavorable treatment conditional on a counterpart's prior treatment. & \citet{BoltonOckenfels2000}; \citet{CharnessRabin2002}; \citet{FalkEtAl2018} \\
C17 & \textbf{Endgame urgency}. Increase in willingness to trade, compromise, or accept modest gains as opportunities run out. & \citet{Rubinstein1982} \\

C18 & \textbf{Breakdown tolerance}. Willingness to risk ending with few or no trades rather than accept modest gains or moderate claims. & \citet{Rubinstein1982}; \citet{StraubMurnighan1995}; \citet{FalkEtAl2018} \\

C19 & \textbf{Own-payoff computation accuracy}. Accuracy in calculating payoffs using private chip values and checking whether trades are possible with the available chips. & \citet{Guth1982}; \citet{KagelEtAl1996} \\

C20 & \textbf{Feedback-based strategic adaptation}. Degree to which offers and responses change coherently following acceptance, rejection, and payoff feedback. & \citet{ErevRoth1998}; \citet{Rubinstein1982} \\

rows: B01 & \textbf{Strategic iteration depth}. How strongly an observed request supports successive reasoning about the opponent's response. & \citet{AradRubinstein2012,Nagel1995,CamererHoChong2004} \\

B02 & \textbf{Opponent-belief sophistication and hedging}. How strongly an observed request supports a response to uncertainty about the opponent's choice. & \citet{GoereeLouisZhang2018,AradRubinstein2012} \\

B03 & \textbf{Payoff and incentive sensitivity}. The extent to which an observed request reflects the material payoff consequences of the stated rule. & \citet{McKelveyPalfrey1995,ManningHorton2025} \\
B04 & \textbf{Upper-endpoint salience}. The extent to which an observed request suggests attraction to the upper endpoint beyond what payoff incentives explain. & \citet{AradRubinstein2012} \\
B05 & \textbf{Payoff-computation precision}. How precisely an observed request follows a payoff-relevant best response or rule-specific target. & \citet{GoereeLouisZhang2018,McKelveyPalfrey1995} \\
B06 & \textbf{Bonus pursuit versus security}. The extent to which an observed request sacrifices secure base payoff to pursue the contingent bonus. & \citet{LiRong2018,ManningHorton2025} \\

B07 & \textbf{Instruction comprehension and adherence}. The consistency of the observed request and associated comprehension checks with the stated rules. & Feature assessing understanding of the game instructions; not a personality construct \\
